South Florida for the most part, but I've lived all over the country.
South Florida, Central Florida, Orlando, Gainesville, back to Indiana, South Bend, Las Vegas for 10 years, Memphis for six years, here for six years, Phoenix for four years.
So the past six years.
Oxford, Mississippi for three years.
So you've been in a lot of places.
Yeah.
Excellent.
What are some of your favorite places that you've lived so far?
Vegas probably.
Really?
Yeah, if it weren't for X, Ys, I'd still be there.
If what?

What attracted you?
I've been to Vegas once, but what attracted you to Vegas?
Well, I got a job up.

Okay.
Vegas and Knight County.
What's that?
Vegas and Knight County, which is suburban next door.
Right, right.
So where does the film and radio come in?
Well, I ran for office a couple of times.
I've always been politically active.
That's basically all I do now is work on political campaigns.
And before I went to law school, I worked with jobs in public administration or education.
That required me to do interview talk shows, that sort of thing.
Do you like doing that sort of work?
Oh yeah, I'm a ham.
I sing karaoke once or twice a week.
I've been in the...
Four movies or did one episode of It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia.

But yeah, I like public speaking.
Always have.
Yeah?
Yeah.
How about, have you ever run for, have you ever held office besides public defender?
Well, I'm a state public defender.
I was the director of the Palm Beach County Division of Senior Services, which is a government
It's a joint federal state, or state, actually joint federal county department for seniors.
It's funded by the Older Americans Act.
You've got them here, but ours was all government run, and it was all in one big program.
As to here, you've got independent little branches that are run by nonprofits.
The other two times I ran for elected office, I lost, which is one of the reasons I'm here.
I ran for district attorney in my county in 98, I think it was.
I don't know what I was thinking.
I think I was drunk most of the time out there.
I got married twice and ran for district attorney against an incumbent member of my own party.
I don't know what the hell I was thinking about that.
I did pretty well, though.
The other time I ran for justice court judge, which is equivalent to your...
County court or municipal court judge, I suppose, here.
And that was a disaster.
That was a, it was a nonpartisan election, but it turned out to be highly political.
And it was just awful.
There was nothing left of my practice by the time I was done with the campaign after losing.
And which, then I went, my mother was sick, and then I went back, so I went back to South Florida.
Why am I just telling you that that wasn't the question?
That's fine.
That's right.
Right.
If you keep talking, that's good.
We're just trying to elicit some stuff.
Yeah, well, I went back to Florida to take care of my mother, who had cancer.
And then she died in 2002.
I went back to Memphis and worked on a death penalty case for a year or so.
And then I came out here to work for DuPont, who screwed me on an appellate matter.
And then I haven't left.
And I've been doing mostly political stuff from that point.
I'll do a little legal stuff from time to time.
But mostly it's campaigning for more progressive causes.
Communist in real life.
Really?
Yeah, but Democrats are close enough.
It's as close as I'm going to get.
How do you feel as a political outlier in this society?
Because I wouldn't say that I have any sort of political affiliation at this point.
Yeah.
I mean, I vote Democrat by default.
Right.
But I wouldn't consider myself a Democrat.
In fact, I find myself more and more listening to anarchists.
Yeah, well.
And finding resonance in what they say.
Right, yeah.
So maybe that makes me an anarchist.
I don't know.
Or a nihilist, one of the two.
But how do you feel politically as a...
No, I really am a Marxist.
And the core of all problems in this country, domestic, international,
are all rooted in economics, in particular the way that people are, that wealth is distributed in this country.
The problem in the Western world, it gets worse all the time, it's been going on since feudalism collapsed.
The problem with capitalism is it values persons in terms of what they own, not what they do.
the imbalance grows between the wealthy and the working people, the less important labor is.
Why do you pay rent in advance, but you get paid after you do the work?
Because no one values labor in this country.
When in fact, as Mark said, I believe that the only thing that has value is labor.
Racism, while it's real, is a creation of...
of the ownership class in order to keep us at each other's throats and away from theirs.
So people who talk about racism in this country, white or black, just irritate the hell out of me.
African American, what the fuck does that mean?
I mean, what does African American mean?
Does it mean Egyptian?
Does it mean that your parents came from Africa?
No.
Does it mean that your ancestors came from Africa?
All of our ancestors came from Africa.
It's a meaningless nonsense term to isolate a particular group of people, which is 11% of the population.
Who cares?
I don't think we should be looking at people that way anyhow, and telling them that somehow they're special.
My ex-wife, my third wife, and mother of my children is black.
I used to say, well, it's black, but she still is.
And my children, who I'm very close to, in fact, I'm trying to get my son to move out.
He's in Vegas now.
He's in the Army.
Trying to get him to move out here to get him into school.
And my daughter lives right over the river, and I'm very close to my children.
When anyone asks, what I've taught them is when anyone asks what your race is, say what I do, which is short distances only.

I'm making too big of a deal, but I think it's important because it is, as I say, one of the major factors to distract working people and to keep them from uniting by saying, no, it's called whitey done it.
Well, whitey didn't do shit.
I didn't do anything.
I never owned any slaves.
No one I know owned any slaves.
Your ancestors were slaves, so were mine.
You know, I'm Irish.
You know, everybody's was.
Slavery's not 400 years old.
Where they get that number is beyond me.
But slavery's not 400 years old anyway.
Slavery is 10,000 years old.
There's always been slaves.
It's a function.
Humanity or civilization, not humans, but civilization.
Or just that some civilizations have always depended to one degree or another on slavery.
And if you look at it really, what's happening in capitalist countries is that they're still depending on slavery.
That would be us.
They give us enough to keep us from starving to death in most countries.
But that's all.
You know, in the meantime, you've got people like Bill Gates with, you know how long it would take to spend a billion dollars if you spent a dollar a second?
If you spent a dollar a second 24-7, you know how long it would take you to spend a billion dollars?
How long?
30 years.
He's got $50 billion.
How do we allow that?
What is the point of that?
Not to mention, I mean, he's...
His fortune is also based off of things that he didn't create, but instead marketed and made money off of.
Well, I don't care about that.
Anything that's a product of someone's labor, that's fine, but he's controlling resources he can't possibly use.
Right.
Well, and I was merely saying his programs are based off of Steve Jobs, and even Steve Jobs'stuff is based off of the Unix programming.
All that stuff is based off of one guy, and that guy's not making any money off of it because he made it free.
Yeah, and it's no longer a product of his labor.
Now it's a product of his ownership.
Yeah, exactly.

It's just wrong.

Yeah.

Oh, yeah.

I mean, you know, really.
Why would the NAACP be interested in that?
Everything gets converted into a race issue.
It's not a race issue.
It has to do with a criminal.

But, you know, as to whether he should be allowed to play football, I don't see why not.
I mean, he served his time.
All right, so what?
So, as long as he's not around.
As far as I know, the dogs are not involved in football games.
I don't know if I'd want them at Mississippi State or the University of Georgia near the mascot.
But the point is, why would the NAACP get involved in that?
That's just stupid.
I mean, you can understand PETA.
Those people are crazy, by the way.

People for the eating of tasty animals.
We're supposed to consume meat.
You get sick if you don't eat meat.
And that's whatever.
I can't imagine.

True.
You know, that would be horrible.

It wasn't me.

I mean, we always combine these.

Not much.
A few chromosomes here and there.
Not much.
You'll be consistent.
So, it's your...

Dick Gregory was, he's like, he's close to 80 by now, but he was a black comedian and at one time was a,
black power type person that's back in the 60s or early 70s, but he became a vegetarian and then someone pointed out to him that he was murdering innocent crops and stuff.
So he became a fruitarian because you can pick the fruit but it doesn't kill the tree.
So, well, maybe so, but do individual tomatoes, you know, attack and kill tomatoes.
Do individual tomatoes have feelings?
I don't know.

Well, yeah.

So, well, anyway.

Flagstaff.

Why is that?
It has amazing weather.
Never gets over 95, I think 97 degrees is the highest temperature on record.
So it's up at 7,000 feet.
It's not like most of Arizona.
It's nice and cool.
It's a pine forest.
It's the gateway to the Grand Canyon sort of thing.
Just amazing weather.
It's beautiful there.
There's no pollution.
Well, because it all blows onto the reservation.
I don't know.
It's a great town.
DC was fun.
I had a really good time living there.
It's always something to do.

It was the first time I'd lived on the East Coast, so it was a huge experiential thing for me as well.
And I was in the Army, so everything was free, which makes D.C.
A lot easier to enjoy.
I can imagine.
Any big city, really.
Like, if someone's paying your rent, paying for your clothes, and paying for your food, it's a hell of a lot easier to have a really good time.
You're the second person I've talked to.
Well, the first person I've talked to who is in the Marines.
Oh, okay.

My experience in the Army was, I mean, I'm not going to say that it wasn't hard and there weren't times that I fucking hated it, but it was good for me.
You know, I joined when I was 21, and I'd like to say that I grew up in the relative safety of the arms of the federal government.
You know, because you can't really fuck up that much.
They're constantly looking over your shoulder.
They tell you, you know, time and time and time and time again, don't do this, don't do this, don't do this.
You know, don't overdraw your checking account.
You could get in trouble.
You know, don't...
Don't go down into the red zone because there's more AIDS in this country than there is in like 90% of the world, you know.
And they hammer it into you.
So it's like your parents are always there.
Only you learned to tune your parents out when you were nine, and these are drill sergeants and, you know, other people that you haven't learned to tune out yet.
So, well, that, you know, you could end up in jail.
So those things, you know, tend to motivate you to not do as many stupid things as much, I guess.
So, yeah, it was a good experience for me.
You know, I had a job I couldn't quit, and money coming in, but, you know, when I was broke, I was broke, and I don't know, it was good for me.
Do you, what motivated you in the first place to go to the young?
I needed a job I couldn't quit, and I wanted to get out of Phoenix.
I was, you know, like I said, I was 21 years old, and I'd been going to the bar since I was 19.
And I would see the same people there, you know, because it was like the same neighborhood bar and go with the same group of people and see the same people.
And people that were the age that I was when I got out at the time, you know, who were working crappy jobs just so they could go to the bar and drink every night.
And I just didn't want that.
I was afraid of getting trapped.
You know, I mean, Phoenix is a big city, relatively speaking.
But where I was at the time felt a lot like a small town, and I was afraid of getting stuck there.
So the military was my way out.
Have you worked in other areas?
Yeah.
I've worked mostly in patient care.

Career-wise.
Yeah.

Like, that's, like, the best place to be.

So I went to school.
In San Antonio, that's what I was doing there.
For that time period, I was going to school.

So I worked in psych for five years, and it was good, you know, but I realized, like, when I got out, that psych wasn't for me because I talked too much.
Like, therapy is more about them talking, you know.
And then when I got out, I immediately went to Honeywell Inc., which isn't huge out here.
Well, it's huge in that West.

And that's the stuff that you're used to seeing with a Honeywell name on it.
But they also make black boxes and nose cones and generators.
And, I mean, they're huge, multibillion-dollar, multinational corporation.
They're humongous.
They just aren't a lot of plants out here.
I don't know why, but in Phoenix there's like 14 plants.
They make defense systems.
My dad worked for Honeywell when he got out of the Air Force, which is what took us to Phoenix from Colorado.

That's what brought me out here.
What exactly made you miserable?
Because I mean, I've worked jobs where it's like, like I worked at Wharton.
where the pay was much better than it was here, but I absolutely couldn't stay in that environment.
Well, for me, it was making a difference.

and helping.

You stay.

And we ended up...
A few of us got together.

So that's pretty much how it went.
And we just sort of, it was sort of like a vigil until her dad called and then...

And it was just...
It was eerie.
It was surreal.
